target_customer: Families and professional caregivers of elders, people with disabilities and people in recovery
problem: Elders lose billions to scams and fraud and banks cannot reverse payments, while caregivers lack controls that preserve independence.
business_model: fintech with prepaid card and account fees and interchange, later investment and family banking products
product_category: protected prepaid card and family banking

founders.name: Kai Stinchcombe
founders.background_notes: Started after his grandmother wrote up to 75 checks a month to fake charities (TechCrunch, 2013-08-01).

founders.name: Claire McDonnell
founders.background_notes: Leads product per TechCrunch; a FinSMEs snippet calls her co-founder.

technical_complexity.rationale: Required a bank issuer and processor partnership (Sunrise Banks, i2c) and custom fraud blocking rules.

defensibility.rationale: Bank partnerships and compliance plus family workflows are harder to copy than the card itself.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent copied the wedge that was found; the company grew and in 2016 acquired Next Step Network.

market_need_then: A MetLife study cited in 2013 coverage put elder financial abuse losses at about $2.9 billion a year.

identity.logo: A T mark beside the True Link wordmark, per a third party profile
identity.voice_and_tone: caring, values driven (humility, inclusion, caring, ambition, excellence)

branding.community_and_virality: Named to the Forbes Fintech 50 two years running, per a 2026 press release.

brand_strength.rationale: Trusted niche brand with Forbes Fintech 50 recognition, but no evidence of viral pull.

pivots.to: broader financial services for people with complex needs and their caregivers
pivots.why: Company states it now serves people in recovery, people with disabilities and caregivers; date approximate from 2020 funding announcement.

outcome_analysis: True Link began as a protected prepaid card for elders after the CEO's grandmother was scammed and broadened to people with complex needs. It raised a $35 million Series B in July 2020 from Khosla and Centana, claims over 250,000 families served and was named to the Forbes Fintech 50. Founder market fit and bank partnerships helped; earlier round history was not found.
notes: One outlet snippet said a smaller $21M Series B from Khosla came about 14 months earlier (roughly 2019); single source, unverified, not recorded. No Series A found. The 2013 TechCrunch article names no competitors; a search snippet mentioned the AARP card in passing, not verifiable. Founder education and employers not found. YC page and company site give founding year 2012 and 2013 variously.
